To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
executive function, processing, and response variability might be endophenotypes of ADHD.

(a) the ADHD subjects in our sample are significantly impaired on executive function, response variability and processing speed tasks, (b) unaffected co-twins of ADHD subjects are similarly impaired on nearly all of the same tasks as their ADHD siblings (even when subclinical symptoms are controlled), and (c) the ADHD subjects are not significantly impaired on measures of arousal and motivation/delay aversiveness.

(1) the neuropsychological deficits of ADHD subjects extend beyond executive function to include processing speed and response variability; and (2) unaffected co twins of ADHD siblings are significantly impaired in the same areas as their affected siblings.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ADHD is a disorder of executive functions and that these deficits are present in both ADHD children and their unaffected siblings.
the executive dysfunction hypothesis of ADHD is a viable hypothesis that has been supported by a number of studies.
the neuropsychological deficits in ADHD are not specific to the disorder.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ADHD subjects show impairment on executive function (e.g., working memory, inhibition, and planning), processing speed (i.e., speed of information processing), and response variability measures (e.g., response time variability, variability in response accuracy) relative to control subjects.
ADHD is a disorder of executive function and that executive function deficits are a useful endophenotype for genetic studies.
ADHD is a complex genetic condition with a large number of genetic and environmental factors that contribute to its expression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neuropsychological deficits associated with ADHD are not limited to those who have the disorder, but extend to the unaffected siblings of children with ADHD.
the deficits we found in ADHD children were also present in unaffected siblings, and this was true even when the sibling had subclinical symptoms of the disorder.
there is evidence for a shared genetic liability to ADHD and to neuropsychological deficits that might underlie ADHD symptoms.
